content: Potassium iodate (KIO3) is a chemical compound with specific applications in both medical and industrial contexts. In the field of radiation treatment, potassium iodate is sometimes utilized due to its ability to displace radioactive iodine from the thyroid gland, thereby reducing the risk of radiation-induced thyroid damage. For further details on this application, one may refer to potassium iodide, which is also used for similar purposes. In the baking industry, potassium iodate is occasionally employed as a maturing agent, similar to potassium bromate. Its role as an oxidizing agent makes it effective in this capacity. However, due to its oxidizing properties, potassium iodate poses a fire hazard when it comes into contact with combustible materials or reducing agents. The compound can be synthesized through a chemical reaction involving a potassium-containing base, such as potassium hydroxide, and iodic acid. The reaction proceeds as follows: HI03 + KOH → KIO3 + H2O. Alternatively, potassium iodate can be prepared by adding iodine to a hot, concentrated solution of potassium hydroxide, as demonstrated in the reaction: 3 I2 + 6 KOH → KIO3 + 5 KI + 3 H2O. It is critical to avoid exposing potassium iodate to certain conditions or substances, as these can lead to hazardous reactions. Specifically, it should not come into contact with heat, shock, friction, combustible materials, reducing agents, aluminum, organic compounds, carbon, hydrogen peroxide, or sulfides. In terms of its use, potassium iodate is commonly employed in the iodination of salt. This is because potassium iodide, another iodine source, can be oxidized to iodine under wet conditions in the presence of oxygen. To prevent this oxidation, companies in the United States often add thiosulfates or other antioxidants to potassium iodide. In contrast, some other countries prefer to use potassium iodate as the iodine source in salt iodination due to its stability under such conditions.
